options.rationale: The candidate accepts the information gap as permanent and uses it to justify the lock-in it causes. The city would pay a non-competitive price precisely because it never took possession of what it owns.

options.text: Ask the incumbent to run a briefing day for prospective bidders, explaining the architecture and the remaining backlog before they submit their bids.
options.rationale: The candidate improves access but leaves the incumbent controlling what is shown and how. A competitor's briefing is a poor substitute for direct access to material the city owns outright.

options.text: Bring the code, backlog and documentation into the city's own repositories and make them available to every bidder, with time allowed to examine them.
options.rationale: The incumbent's advantage comes from holding information the city already owns. Taking it into the city's custody and opening it equally to all bidders makes the competition real and reduces the city's dependence whoever wins.

questions.explanation: An incumbent's advantage in a re-tender usually comes from controlling information that the buyer already owns. Taking that material into the buyer's own custody and opening it equally to every bidder is what turns a nominal competition into a real one, and it lowers the buyer's dependence whatever the result. Excluding the incumbent, or giving up on competition, treats an information gap as if it were a fixed fact about the market.
questions.mindset: Own your project's knowledge in practice, not just on paper, so that competition stays possible.

questions.stem: A vendor team is building a membership platform for a sports federation under a time-and-materials contract with a not-to-exceed ceiling of £600,000. After nine of fourteen planned sprints, £480,000 has been invoiced, and the product owner estimates that 35% of the must-have backlog remains. At the current burn rate the ceiling will be reached around sprint twelve. Which two actions should the project manager take now?

options.text: Show the sponsor the forecast and the options — reduced scope, a higher ceiling or a later release — while there is still time to choose between them.
options.rationale: Whether to cut scope, add money or move the date is the sponsor's trade-off, and the ceiling is valuable precisely because it warns in time. Three sprints out, every option is still open; at sprint twelve most of them are gone.

options.text: Work with the product owner to re-slice and re-rank the remaining must-haves, so that the money left buys the highest-value increments first.
options.rationale: Whatever the sponsor decides, the remaining budget should go to the most valuable work. Re-slicing often reveals that part of each must-have delivers most of its value, which widens the sponsor's options.

options.text: Ask the vendor to keep the team working beyond the ceiling at its own risk, on the understanding that the overrun will be settled at the end.
options.rationale: The candidate invites work outside the contract's limit with no authority to pay for it. The ceiling exists to stop exactly this, and an informal understanding becomes a dispute when the bill arrives.

options.text: Propose converting the remaining work to a firm fixed price, so that the vendor carries the risk of the backlog taking longer than estimated.
options.rationale: The candidate expects a contract change to remove uncertainty. A fixed price for a backlog still being re-sliced will be priced with a heavy contingency or argued over, and negotiating it eats the time the decision needs.

options.text: Reduce the vendor team by two developers for the remaining sprints, so that the burn rate falls and the ceiling is not reached before sprint fourteen.
options.rationale: The candidate manages the burn rate instead of the value. A smaller team spreads the same money over more sprints but delivers less in each, so the gap between scope and budget is unchanged and simply arrives later.

questions.explanation: A not-to-exceed ceiling on a time-and-materials contract is a budget control, and its worth lies in the early warning it gives. When the forecast shows the ceiling arriving before the scope, the decision belongs to the sponsor and should be put to them while options still exist, and the backlog should be re-sliced so that the remaining money buys the most value. Asking the supplier to work past the limit, changing contract form mid-stream or merely slowing the spend all leave the real trade-off unmade.
questions.mindset: Surface a ceiling breach while it is still a choice, and spend what is left on what matters most.

questions.stem: A supplier of offshore wind-turbine towers tells you that delivery of six towers will be five weeks late because a strike at its export port has stopped all loading. It claims force majeure, which under the contract excuses delay caused by events beyond the supplier's reasonable control, provided notice is given within ten days and the supplier takes reasonable steps to reduce the effect. Which two should you establish before accepting or rejecting the claim?

options.text: Whether the supplier's notice reached you within ten days of the strike first affecting its deliveries.
options.rationale: Notice is a condition of the relief, not a courtesy. A late notice can defeat an otherwise valid claim, and the date the event began to bite is the one the clause measures from.

options.text: Whether the supplier has explored reasonable alternatives, such as loading at another port, to cut the delay.
options.rationale: The clause excuses only the delay the supplier could not reasonably avoid. If another port could have shortened it, relief extends only to the delay that would have remained.

options.text: Whether the strike has made the contract unprofitable for the supplier, since that would strengthen its case for relief.
options.rationale: The candidate confuses hardship with force majeure. The clause concerns events that prevent or delay performance; an event that only makes performance more expensive is not what it excuses.

options.text: Whether the supplier's other customers have also been told that their deliveries will be late because of the strike.
options.rationale: The candidate looks for consistency rather than compliance. How the supplier has treated other customers says nothing about whether this claim meets the conditions in this contract.

options.text: Whether the supplier's insurance covers losses from the strike, so that it can claim against its policy for your extra costs.
options.rationale: The candidate turns a question of excusing delay into one of recovering cost. The supplier's insurance is its own arrangement, and a force majeure clause typically relieves liability rather than creating compensation.

questions.explanation: A force majeure clause is a set of conditions, and a claim under it is tested against each one: whether the event is of the kind the clause covers, whether notice was given as required, and whether the affected party has done what it reasonably can to limit the effect. Higher cost, other customers' experience and insurance arrangements are not tests the clause applies. Checking the conditions before responding keeps the decision tied to the contract rather than to sympathy or suspicion.
questions.mindset: Test a relief claim against the clause's conditions, one by one, before deciding how you feel about it.

questions.stem: Your hospital trust has chosen a contractor to build a modular operating theatre, with the structure delivered to a fixed design and the clinical fit-out refined with surgeons in iterations. Contract terms will take six more weeks to agree, but the factory slot for the modules will be lost unless design and long-lead orders start now. The sponsor approves a letter of intent. Which two should the letter contain?

options.text: A cap on the total the trust will pay for work done under the letter if the full contract is ultimately not signed.
options.rationale: The cap fixes the trust's maximum exposure if negotiations fail. Without it, the letter becomes an open-ended commitment to pay for whatever the contractor does in the meantime.

options.text: A defined list of the preliminary work authorised, limited to design and the long-lead orders needed to hold the factory slot.
options.rationale: Authorising only what the time pressure requires keeps the letter proportionate to its purpose, and makes clear that anything beyond that list waits for the signed contract.

options.text: A commitment to award the full contract to the contractor once negotiations are complete, to give it confidence to start.
options.rationale: The candidate turns a holding instrument into a binding award before the terms are settled, giving away the trust's leverage over everything still being negotiated.

options.text: Agreement that the contractor's standard terms will govern the preliminary work until the full contract has been signed.
options.rationale: The candidate fills the gap with the other party's paper. The work done under the letter is the work most likely to be disputed if talks fail, and it would be judged on terms drafted for the contractor.

options.text: An instruction to start the whole of the works now, so that the six weeks of negotiation do not hold up the overall programme.
options.rationale: The candidate maximises speed by maximising exposure. Starting everything while the terms are open commits the trust to the whole project without any of the protections the contract is being negotiated to provide.

questions.explanation: A letter of intent buys time by authorising some work before the contract is agreed, and its job is to limit the buyer's exposure if agreement never comes. It does so by naming exactly which preliminary work is authorised and capping what will be paid for it, while leaving the main negotiation open. The more a letter commits — to the award, to the whole scope, to the other side's terms — the more it becomes a contract without the protections of one.
questions.mindset: When you must start before signing, authorise only what time demands and cap what it can cost.

questions.stem: A telecoms company is outsourcing its billing platform to a vendor for five years; cutover follows a fixed plan and enhancements are then delivered in sprints. The commercial manager is drafting the contract and has three concerns from the steering group. Match each concern to the clause that addresses it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: If the vendor fails financially, the company could lose access to the software that runs its billing.
A planned merger may make the outsourced platform unnecessary in two years, however well the vendor performs.
When the contract ends, customer data and configuration must move to whoever runs billing next without disruption.

options.text: Source code escrow with defined release triggers
options.rationale: Escrow places the code with an independent agent and releases it to the buyer on named events such as insolvency, so the company can keep its billing running without the vendor.

options.text: Termination for convenience with an agreed compensation schedule
options.rationale: The merger is a change in the buyer's own needs, not a failure by the vendor. A right to end the contract without proving fault, at a cost agreed in advance, is the clause written for that.

options.text: Exit assistance obligations, including data return in an agreed format
options.rationale: An orderly handover needs the vendor's cooperation at the very moment it is losing the business, so the obligation to assist and to return data in a usable form has to be agreed while both sides still want the contract.

options.text: Liquidated damages for late delivery of milestones
options.rationale: Not used. Liquidated damages compensate for lateness against agreed milestones, and none of the three concerns is about delay: they are about failure, a change of need and the end of the relationship.

questions.explanation: Contract clauses are risk responses written in advance, and each answers a specific question about what happens if something goes wrong. Supplier failure is met by securing what the buyer needs to carry on without the supplier; a change in the buyer's own needs by a right to end the contract without proving fault, at a pre-agreed cost; and the end of the relationship by obligations that make the transfer workable. Matching clause to risk at drafting stage is far cheaper than negotiating any of these after the event.
questions.mindset: Write the failure and exit routes into a contract while both parties still want to sign it.

questions.stem: You are negotiating a 12-month extension with the vendor that supplies two Scrum teams for your energy retailer's customer platform. Three moments from the sessions are below. Match each to the response that best protects your position. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: With the day rate agreed, the vendor's lead adds, as a final small point, a 5% uplift for weekend support cover.
The vendor's negotiator says he can agree the service credits only once his managing director signs them off next month.
The vendor says its rate is available only if the extension is signed by Friday, four weeks before the current contract ends.

options.text: Treat it as reopening the package and ask what the vendor will give in return
options.rationale: A late extra request relies on the agreement feeling finished. Treating it as a new trade, rather than a formality, stops concessions being collected one at a time after the main deal is struck.

options.text: Ask who can approve it and arrange for that person to join the next session
options.rationale: Limited authority lets one side bank your concessions while its own stay provisional. Bringing the real decision-maker into the room puts both sides' commitments on the same footing.

options.text: Test the deadline against your own timetable and alternatives, and decline to be hurried if it has no real basis
options.rationale: With four weeks left on the contract, the pressure is manufactured. Checking it against your real timetable and your alternatives shows whether the deadline costs you anything, and usually it does not.

options.text: Propose splitting the difference so that both sides move by the same amount
options.rationale: Not used. Splitting the difference rewards whichever side opened furthest from a fair figure, and none of these moments is a gap between two positions waiting to be closed.

questions.explanation: Negotiating tactics work by making a concession feel like the natural next step, so the defence is to recognise the move and answer it on its own terms. A late extra demand is answered by treating it as a new trade; a claim of limited authority by bringing the decision-maker into the room; an imposed deadline by testing it against the real timetable and your alternatives. Recognising which tactic is in play is most of the response.
questions.mindset: Name the tactic to yourself before you answer the request it comes wrapped in.

questions.stem: A rail operator's rolling-stock maintenance project buys from many suppliers. The procurement lead is setting a management approach for each supply relationship according to how much is spent and how hard the item is to source. Complete each sentence with the approach that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Brake pads are bought in large volumes from any of six approved suppliers, all able to meet the standard. For this spend, the project should
A £30 door-seal kit is made by only one certified manufacturer, and a train cannot return to service without it. For this item, the project should
Cleaning materials are cheap, standard and stocked by many wholesalers. For these purchases, the project should

options.text: use competition between suppliers to secure the best price and terms
options.rationale: High spend with many capable sources is where competition pays: switching is easy, so the buyer's volume is its leverage and price and terms are where the value lies.

options.text: protect continuity of supply, for example with buffer stock while a second source is qualified
options.rationale: The spend is trivial but the exposure is not: one source and a stopped train. Effort goes into making sure the part is there when needed, not into negotiating a lower price on a £30 kit.

options.text: keep buying simple and cheap to administer, for example through purchasing cards or standing call-offs
options.rationale: Low spend and low risk justify little management attention. The cost of the buying process itself is the main thing to minimise here.

options.text: build a long-term partnership with joint improvement planning and shared targets
options.rationale: Not used. A deep partnership is worth its cost only for items that are both high-spend and hard to source, and none of the three is both.

questions.explanation: Supplier management effort should follow two questions: how much the buyer spends, and how exposed it is if the item cannot be obtained. High spend with many sources rewards competition; low spend with a single critical source calls for protecting supply rather than chasing price; low spend and low risk calls for cheap, simple buying; and only items that are both high-spend and hard to source justify a deep partnership. One approach applied to every supplier wastes effort on some and leaves others unprotected.
questions.mindset: Match the effort you put into a supplier to what you spend and what you would lose without it.

questions.stem: Your stadium project buys structural steel for £2,400,000, a price set at signature. An economic price adjustment clause says 70% of the price moves in proportion to a published steel index and 30% stays fixed. The index stood at 120 at signature. Work out the adjusted price if the index is 138 at delivery, and the adjusted price if it is instead 108.

blanks.label: Adjusted price if the index is 138 at delivery, in £
blanks.rationale: Adjusted price = 2,400,000 × (0.30 + 0.70 × 138 ÷ 120) = 2,400,000 × (0.30 + 0.805) = 2,400,000 × 1.105 = £2,652,000. The index rose 15%, but only 70% of the price follows it, so the price rises 10.5%.

blanks.label: Adjusted price if the index is 108 at delivery, in £
blanks.rationale: Adjusted price = 2,400,000 × (0.30 + 0.70 × 108 ÷ 120) = 2,400,000 × (0.30 + 0.63) = 2,400,000 × 0.93 = £2,232,000. The clause works in both directions, so a 10% fall in the index cuts the price by 7%.

blanks.label: Which party carries the steel market-price risk on the indexed 70% — buyer or supplier
blanks.rationale: The indexed share moves with the market whichever way it goes, so the buyer pays more when steel rises and less when it falls. The supplier keeps the risk on the fixed 30% and on any gap between its own costs and the index.

questions.explanation: An economic price adjustment clause moves part of a fixed price with a published index, shifting the market-price risk on that part from the supplier to the buyer. The adjusted price is the fixed share plus the indexed share scaled by the ratio of the current index to the base index, and the clause cuts both ways. Buyers use it on long contracts for volatile commodities because, without it, suppliers price the volatility in as contingency whether or not it ever materialises.
questions.mindset: Know which way an index clause cuts, because it is meant to cut both ways.

questions.stem: A water treatment plant is buying filtration equipment for €1.6 million; the civil works follow a fixed plan while the control software is delivered iteratively. The preferred supplier's proposed payment schedule is shown, giving each milestone's share of the price beside its share of the work in the engineer's estimate. Select the milestone that should be renegotiated before signing because it leaves the buyer most exposed if the supplier fails.

graphic.title: Proposed payment schedule: five milestones, each with its share of price and share of work
graphic.caption: Select a milestone. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Mobilisation and design approval — 25% of price; 8% of work
regions.rationale: The buyer would pay €400,000 for work worth about €128,000, so €272,000 is at risk before anything has been built. Cumulative payment runs furthest ahead of cumulative work here, and nothing exists yet that the buyer could keep.

regions.label: Off-site fabrication — 30% of price; 42% of work
regions.rationale: This milestone pays less than the work it covers, so it reduces the buyer's exposure: cumulatively 55% paid against 50% of work. Choosing it confuses the largest payment with the largest risk.

regions.label: Delivery to site — 20% of price; 15% of work
regions.rationale: It pays slightly ahead of the work, taking cumulative exposure to 10 points (75% paid, 65% done), but that is well below the 17 points opened up at the first milestone, and the equipment is on site by then.

regions.label: Installation and integration — 15% of price; 25% of work
regions.rationale: Payment lags the work here, bringing cumulative payment and work level at 90%. It is the milestone where the supplier carries the most risk, not the buyer.

regions.label: Commissioning and acceptance — 10% of price; 10% of work
regions.rationale: Payment and work are in step, and the final payment is held until acceptance. This is the protection the buyer wants, so there is nothing here to renegotiate.

questions.explanation: A payment schedule decides how much of the buyer's money is at risk at each point in a contract: paying ahead of the work delivered amounts to an unsecured loan to the supplier. The milestone to challenge is the one where cumulative payment runs furthest ahead of cumulative work, which is usually early, when little exists that the buyer could keep. Rebalancing it, or securing it with an advance payment bond, is far easier before signature than after.
questions.mindset: Pay in step with the value delivered, so that a supplier's failure costs you time rather than money.
